renaissance.name: The Renaissance

intro.title: A rebirth
intro.text: Italy, around 1400 to 1600. Artists revived the ideas of ancient Greece and Rome and put people, not just God, at the centre.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Deep, mathematically correct perspective. Calm, balanced groups. Real-looking bodies, studied from life.

intro.title: The big names
intro.text: Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael in Florence and Rome. Titian in Venice. North of the Alps: van Eyck, Holbein, Bosch, Bruegel.

questions.q: 'Renaissance' means…
questions.explain: French for rebirth: the revival of classical learning and art.

questions.q: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
questions.explain: Florence in particular, funded by families like the Medici.

questions.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explain: Leonardo, from about 1503. It's in the Louvre.

questions.q: Who painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling?
questions.explain: Michelangelo, 1508–12. He saw himself as a sculptor first.

questions.q: What did Renaissance painters use to make space look deep and real?
questions.explain: Lines converging on a vanishing point. Brunelleschi worked it out in Florence in the early 1400s.

questions.q: Leonardo's soft, smoky blending of edges is called…
questions.explain: From the Italian for smoke. Look at the corners of the Mona Lisa's mouth.

questions.q: Venice and Florence had different priorities. Venice prized…
questions.explain: Florence praised disegno (drawing); Venice, led by Titian, praised colore.

questions.q: What's hidden across the floor of Holbein's The Ambassadors?
questions.explain: An anamorphic skull: view it from the side and it snaps into shape. A reminder of death.

questions.q: Where can you see The Birth of Venus?
questions.explain: In the Uffizi, along with Botticelli's Primavera.

questions.q: In The School of Athens, who is said to have Leonardo's face?
questions.explain: Plato, pointing upwards, at the centre.

questions.q: Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow belongs to a series showing…
questions.explain: Probably six scenes of the farming year, painted in 1565. Five survive; three are in Vienna.

2.title: Rebirth
2.text: Renaissance means ‘rebirth’. From about 1400, Italian artists and scholars looked back to ancient Greece and Rome, and rich patrons like the Medici family in Florence paid for new art to show off their wealth and faith.

2.title: New tools
2.text: Painters worked out linear perspective, so a flat wall seemed to open into deep space, and studied anatomy to make bodies convincing. Leonardo even dissected corpses to understand how muscles work.

2.title: North and south
2.text: In Italy many artists painted frescoes on wet plaster. In the north, Flemish painters like Jan van Eyck perfected oil paint, building up glowing detail in thin layers. Ideas travelled in both directions.

renaissance.look: calm, balanced pictures with convincing perspective and anatomy, inspired by ancient Greece and Rome

van-eyck.name: Jan van Eyck

intro.title: Who was he?
intro.text: A Flemish painter of the first half of the 1400s, based in Bruges and court painter to the Duke of Burgundy. His faces are so lifelike you can see every wrinkle and hint of stubble.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: 'Van Eyck: The Portraits' at the National Gallery, 21 November 2026 to 11 April 2027, gathers his surviving portraits together for the first time.

intro.title: Oil magic
intro.text: He perfected oil glazes: thin transparent layers that make fur, metal, skin and light glow. Look at every reflection.

questions.q: Where did Jan van Eyck work?
questions.explain: Bruges, in today's Belgium, the great trading city of the 1400s.

questions.q: Which of his paintings hangs in the National Gallery, London?
options: The Madonna of Canon van der Paele
questions.explain: Bought in 1842. In the new show it hangs for the first time beside a Berlin portrait that may show the same man.

questions.q: Van Eyck is famous for mastering which material?
questions.explain: He didn't invent oil paint, but he took it further than anyone before him.

questions.q: What's the hallmark of a van Eyck painting?
questions.explain: You can count the hairs in the fur and see windows reflected in the mirror.

questions.q: Van Eyck's motto, painted on frames, was…
questions.explain: A pun on his name: 'As I/Eyck can'.

questions.q: What's on the back wall of the Arnolfini Portrait?
options: A convex mirror reflecting two more people
questions.explain: Above it he wrote, in Latin: 'Jan van Eyck was here 1434'.

questions.q: Which great altarpiece did he complete in 1432?
questions.explain: Begun by his brother Hubert (died 1426) and finished by Jan. It's in St Bavo's Cathedral, Ghent.

questions.q: The man in the red turban (National Gallery, London) may be…
questions.explain: Many think it's a self-portrait; the frame carries his motto.

questions.q: Van Eyck was court painter to which ruler?
options: Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy
questions.explain: He joined Philip's court in 1425 and even went on secret missions for him.

questions.q: Which panel of the Ghent Altarpiece was stolen in 1934 and has never been found?
options: The Adoration of the Mystic Lamb
questions.explain: The panel in place today is a copy, painted in the 1940s.

van-eyck.look: minutely detailed oil paintings with glowing colour

baroque.name: Baroque

intro.title: Drama
intro.text: The 1600s wanted art you feel in your stomach: diagonal movement, big emotion, a frozen moment of action.

intro.title: Light out of darkness
intro.text: Caravaggio lit figures like a spotlight in a dark room. The style spread across Europe.

intro.title: The Dutch Golden Age
intro.text: Protestant Holland went quieter: portraits, interiors, still lifes. Rembrandt in Amsterdam, Vermeer in Delft.

questions.q: Roughly when was the Baroque period?
questions.explain: From about 1600 to 1750.

questions.q: Who painted The Night Watch?
questions.explain: Rembrandt, 1642. It's in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

questions.q: Who painted Girl with a Pearl Earring?
questions.explain: Vermeer, about 1665. It's in the Mauritshuis, The Hague.

questions.q: What's the strongest visual sign of Baroque painting?
questions.explain: Chiaroscuro: strong contrast of light and dark.

questions.q: Caravaggio's extreme light-and-dark is called…
questions.explain: From the Italian tenebroso, murky.

questions.q: Vermeer's interiors are usually lit from…
questions.explain: Soft daylight from the left falls across a quiet room.

questions.q: Who appears in the mirror at the back of Las Meninas?
options: The king and queen of Spain
questions.explain: Philip IV and Queen Mariana. Velázquez himself stands at the easel.

questions.q: Where can you see Rembrandt's Self-Portrait with Two Circles for free?
questions.explain: At Kenwood on Hampstead Heath.

questions.q: Artemisia Gentileschi was the first woman admitted to…
questions.explain: In 1616. Her Judith paintings are among the most powerful of the age.

questions.q: Which London painting did a suffragette slash in 1914?
questions.explain: Mary Richardson attacked Velázquez's Venus in the National Gallery. It was repaired.

questions.q: In which three of these places can you see a self-portrait by Rembrandt?
questions.explain: Rembrandt painted around 40 self-portraits, plus many more in etchings and drawings, and they are spread across Europe and the US. Orsay, Tate Modern and the Van Gogh Museum collect much later art.

questions.q: Which three of these Vermeers belong to the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam?
questions.explain: The Rijksmuseum owns four Vermeers, the fourth being Woman Reading a Letter. Girl with a Pearl Earring and View of Delft are at the Mauritshuis in The Hague, and The Art of Painting is in Vienna.

2.title: Art with a mission
2.text: After the Protestant Reformation, the Catholic Church wanted art that moved people and drew them back to the faith. Baroque painters answered with drama, movement and strong light.

2.title: Light and dark
2.text: Caravaggio lit his figures like a spotlight in a dark room. His saints looked like ordinary people from the streets of Rome, which shocked some viewers and thrilled others.

2.title: Two Baroques
2.text: Catholic Spain and Flanders made grand religious and royal pictures, by painters like Velázquez and Rubens. In the Protestant Dutch Republic, buyers wanted portraits, landscapes and everyday scenes for their homes.

baroque.look: drama, movement and strong contrasts of light and dark

rococo.name: Rococo

intro.title: Light and playful
intro.text: After Baroque grandeur, 18th-century France went pastel: flirting aristocrats, swings, dreamy gardens.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Soft pinks and blues, curling decoration, feathery brushwork, pleasure and leisure.

intro.title: Key names
intro.text: Watteau, Boucher and Fragonard. And in London, the Wallace Collection has one of the world's best Rococo collections, free.

questions.q: Rococo flourished mainly in which country?
questions.explain: Paris and the court of Louis XV.

questions.q: Which London museum holds Fragonard's The Swing?
questions.explain: The Wallace Collection, Manchester Square. Free to visit.

questions.q: Which colours feel most Rococo?
questions.explain: Light, sweet and decorative.

questions.q: Rococo paintings are usually about…
questions.explain: Pleasure for an aristocratic audience.

questions.q: The 'fête galante' (elegant outdoor party) was invented for…
questions.explain: The French Academy created the category in 1717 for his Pilgrimage to Cythera.

questions.q: Boucher's most famous patron was…
questions.explain: Louis XV's favourite. The Toilet of Venus was painted for her.

rococo.look: light, playful scenes in soft pastel colours, full of love and leisure

british18c.name: Georgian Britain

intro.title: Britain finds its voice
intro.text: In the 1700s British artists stepped out of the shadow of painters from abroad: satire, society portraits, horses and science.

intro.title: Hogarth and Gainsborough
intro.text: Hogarth told moral stories in picture series. Gainsborough painted elegant portraits set in landscape.

intro.title: Stubbs and Wright
intro.text: Stubbs painted horses with an anatomist's eye. Joseph Wright of Derby painted science by candlelight.

questions.q: Which institution was founded in London in 1768?
questions.explain: With Joshua Reynolds as its first President.

questions.q: George Stubbs is best known for painting…
questions.explain: He dissected horses to publish The Anatomy of the Horse (1766).

questions.q: Hogarth's 'modern moral subjects' tell a story across…
questions.explain: Like A Rake's Progress or Marriage A-la-Mode, which also sold widely as engravings.

questions.q: Gainsborough's portraits often place sitters…
options: In front of a black background
questions.explain: He loved landscape and painted it with feathery brushwork.

questions.q: What's unfinished in Mr and Mrs Andrews?
questions.explain: An empty patch where something, maybe a bird or a child, was planned.

questions.q: Hogarth's pug was called…
questions.explain: It appears in his self-portrait, The Painter and his Pug.

questions.q: What lights the scene in Wright of Derby's Air Pump painting?
questions.explain: The candle is hidden behind a glass bowl, so faces glow out of the dark like a sacred drama.

british18c.look: elegant portraits of the gentry, conversation pieces and satire

romanticism.name: Romanticism

intro.title: Feeling first
intro.text: A reaction to the Age of Reason: emotion, imagination and the wild power of nature.

intro.title: The sublime
intro.text: Beauty mixed with terror. Storms, mountains and shipwrecks, with tiny humans to show the scale.

intro.title: Key names
intro.text: Turner and Constable in Britain, Friedrich in Germany, Delacroix and Géricault in France, Goya in Spain.

questions.q: Roughly when was Romanticism?
questions.explain: Around the turn of the 19th century.

questions.q: Romantic artists valued above all…
questions.explain: Feeling over reason.

questions.q: Which two British painters are the giants of Romantic landscape?
questions.explain: Turner for drama and light, Constable for the English countryside.

questions.q: The 'sublime' means…
questions.explain: Nature as overwhelming and dangerous.

questions.q: Turner's late style is known for…
options: Swirling light and colour that dissolve shapes
questions.explain: Critics called some of his late pictures 'soapsuds and whitewash'.

questions.q: The Hay Wain was painted by…
questions.explain: In 1821. It shows a scene by Flatford Mill in Suffolk, near Constable's family home, and hangs in the National Gallery.

questions.q: What does The Fighting Temeraire show?
options: A warship towed to be broken up
questions.explain: A Trafalgar veteran pulled by a steam tug: the old age giving way to the new.

questions.q: What tiny animal runs ahead of the train in Rain, Steam and Speed?
questions.explain: Can nature outrun the machine?

questions.q: Liberty Leading the People celebrates the revolution of…
questions.explain: The July Revolution. Delacroix painted it the same year.

questions.q: The Raft of the Medusa was based on…
questions.explain: Géricault interviewed survivors and studied corpses.

romanticism.look: strong emotion, wild nature and the power of the sublime

preraphaelites.name: Pre-Raphaelites

intro.title: A secret brotherhood
intro.text: Founded in London in 1848 by young Royal Academy students, led by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt.

intro.title: Why the name?
intro.text: They rejected the art schools' worship of Raphael and looked to the bright, detailed art before him.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Jewel-bright colour, every leaf painted, stories from Shakespeare, Tennyson and legend. Tate Britain holds the key works.

questions.q: The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood was founded in…
questions.explain: 1848, a year of revolutions across Europe.

questions.q: Where in London are the great Pre-Raphaelite paintings?
questions.explain: Ophelia, The Lady of Shalott, Proserpine and more.

questions.q: Which was NOT a founding member?
questions.explain: Waterhouse came a generation later, borrowing their style.

questions.q: Pre-Raphaelite paintings are known for…
questions.explain: They painted on a wet white ground to make colours glow.

questions.q: Their stories mostly came from…
questions.explain: Shakespeare, Tennyson, Dante, Arthurian legend.

questions.q: Who modelled for Millais' Ophelia?
questions.explain: She lay in a bath of water for hours and caught a bad cold.

questions.q: In Proserpine, what does the pomegranate mean?
options: She must stay in the underworld
questions.explain: Eating its seeds bound her to Hades. The model is Jane Morris.

questions.q: The Lady of Shalott comes from a poem by…
questions.explain: Waterhouse painted it in 1888.

questions.q: Rossetti painted Beata Beatrix in memory of…
questions.explain: Siddal died in 1862. He shows her as Dante's Beatrice, in a trance.

questions.q: Where did Millais hide the letters 'PRB' in Isabella (1849)?
questions.explain: The secret initials of the new Brotherhood. Isabella hangs in the Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool.

questions.q: Rossetti buried a notebook of his poems with Siddal in 1862. What happened seven years later?
options: He had it dug up so he could publish them
His sister rewrote them from memory
questions.explain: The poems came out in 1870.

preraphaelites.look: bright, highly detailed colour and medieval or literary subjects

realism.name: Realism

intro.title: Paint what you see
intro.text: In 1840s France, artists turned from heroes and myths to ordinary people: workers, peasants, funerals.

intro.title: Courbet
intro.text: Gustave Courbet led the charge. He is said to have quipped: 'Show me an angel and I'll paint one.'

intro.title: Manet's scandals
intro.text: Manet took old-master poses and filled them with modern Parisians. Critics were outraged.

questions.q: Realism began in which country?
questions.explain: Around 1848, with Courbet and Millet.

questions.q: Realists chose to paint…
questions.explain: Courbet painted everyday life at the huge size usually kept for history paintings.

questions.q: Why did The Gleaners unsettle some critics?
options: It gave poor labourers heroic dignity
questions.explain: Three poor women gathering leftover grain, painted with the grandeur usually given to heroes. Some read it as political.

questions.q: Which painting shows a modern courtesan in a classic Venus pose?
questions.explain: Manet, 1863, after Titian's Venus of Urbino.

questions.q: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe was shown at the…
questions.explain: The 1863 show of works the official Salon rejected.

questions.q: What happened to Courbet's The Stone Breakers?
questions.explain: It was destroyed in February 1945, in the Second World War, near Dresden.

realism.look: ordinary people and everyday life, shown without idealising them

impressionism.name: Impressionism

intro.title: Light, right now
intro.text: Catching a fleeting moment: sunlight on water, a breezy afternoon, a busy boulevard. Often painted outdoors.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Quick visible brushstrokes, bright unmixed colour, coloured shadows, everyday modern life.

intro.title: A rude name
intro.text: A critic mocked Monet's Impression, Sunrise at the group's first show in Paris in 1874. The insult stuck.

questions.q: The first Impressionist exhibition was held in Paris in…
questions.explain: In the former studio of the photographer Nadar.

questions.q: The movement is named after a painting by…
questions.explain: Impression, Sunrise (1872).

questions.q: Painting 'en plein air' means painting…
questions.explain: New paint tubes made it practical.

questions.q: Which Impressionist was American?
questions.explain: Cassatt, from Pittsburgh, exhibited with the group.

questions.q: Which is most typical of Impressionism?
questions.explain: The brushwork shows: it captures movement and light.

questions.q: How did Impressionists paint shadows?
options: With colour, often blue or violet
questions.explain: Shadows contain colour from the sky and surroundings.

questions.q: Bal du moulin de la Galette shows…
questions.explain: Renoir, 1876, dappled light through trees.

questions.q: Which Manet painting hangs in the Courtauld Gallery, London?
questions.explain: His last major painting, 1882.

questions.q: Gustave Caillebotte also helped the group by…
questions.explain: A wealthy painter, he bought and funded his friends' work.

questions.q: Berthe Morisot exhibited in how many of the eight Impressionist shows?
questions.explain: All but 1879, when she'd just had a daughter.

questions.q: Which three of these artists showed work at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874?
questions.explain: Monet and Morisot were core members, and Cézanne was there too. Manet never showed with the group, Cassatt joined in 1879, and Van Gogh was a 21-year-old art dealer's assistant in London who hadn't started painting yet.

questions.q: Who invited Mary Cassatt to show with the Impressionists?
questions.explain: In 1877. Born near Pittsburgh, she had settled in Paris, and went on to show in four of their exhibitions.

questions.q: When was the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition?
questions.explain: Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte caused a stir there, while Monet and Renoir stayed away.

2.title: Outside the Salon
2.text: In 1874 a group of artists tired of the official Paris Salon put on their own exhibition. A critic mocked Monet's Impression, Sunrise, and the name Impressionists stuck.

2.title: Painting outdoors
2.text: Paint in metal tubes, invented in the 1840s, made it easy to work outside. The Impressionists painted fast to catch changing light, with visible brushstrokes and bright colour.

2.title: Modern life
2.text: Instead of myths and history, they painted the Paris of their own day: cafés, dance halls, railway stations and boating trips.

impressionism.look: quick, visible brushstrokes that catch light and modern life

postimpressionism.name: Post-Impressionism

intro.title: Beyond the moment
intro.text: Artists who started from Impressionism but wanted more: structure, emotion, symbolism.

intro.title: Four routes
intro.text: Cézanne built form from blocks of colour. Van Gogh poured out feeling. Gauguin chased the symbolic. Seurat painted in dots.

intro.title: Named in London
intro.text: The critic Roger Fry coined the term for his 1910 London show. Visitors were outraged.

questions.q: Who coined the term 'Post-Impressionism'?
questions.explain: For 'Manet and the Post-Impressionists' at the Grafton Galleries, London, 1910.

questions.q: Which painter is NOT a Post-Impressionist?
questions.explain: Monet stayed an Impressionist to the end.

questions.q: The Starry Night was painted by…
questions.explain: In 1889, at the asylum in Saint-Rémy. It's at MoMA.

questions.q: Painting with tiny dots of pure colour is called…
questions.explain: Seurat's method, mixed by your eye at a distance.

questions.q: Van Gogh's brushwork is best described as…
questions.explain: He laid paint on thickly, often straight from the tube.

questions.q: Cézanne built his pictures from…
options: Blocks of colour and simple shapes
questions.explain: He said he wanted to treat nature through the cylinder, sphere and cone.

questions.q: Which version of Sunflowers can you see in London?
questions.explain: Painted in Arles in 1888 to decorate Gauguin's room.

questions.q: Gauguin painted Where Do We Come From? in…
questions.explain: In 1897. It reads right to left, from birth to old age.

questions.q: Which Seurat painting is in the National Gallery, London?
options: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
questions.explain: Workers relaxing by the Seine, 1884.

questions.q: Who appears in the background of At the Moulin Rouge?
questions.explain: The short man in the bowler hat.

questions.q: Gauguin died in 1903, far from France, in…
questions.explain: On the island of Hiva Oa in French Polynesia, after years in Tahiti.

2.title: After Impressionism
2.text: By the 1880s some painters felt Impressionism was too much about fleeting light. Post-Impressionism is not one style but a label, coined in 1910 by the critic Roger Fry, for artists who went their own ways.

2.title: Four paths
2.text: Cézanne built solid forms from patches of colour. Seurat used tiny dots. Van Gogh poured feeling into colour and brushwork. Gauguin used flat, symbolic colour.

2.title: Towards modern art
2.text: Cézanne's way of turning nature into simple shapes led on to Cubism, while the bold colour of Van Gogh and Gauguin fed into Fauvism and Expressionism.

postimpressionism.look: bold colour and simplified forms, with each artist going their own way

edo-japan.name: Edo Japan

intro.title: The floating world
intro.text: Ukiyo-e: 'pictures of the floating world'. Actors, beauties, landscapes, sold as cheap woodblock prints.

intro.title: How prints worked
intro.text: A designer drew, a carver cut a block for the outlines and one for each colour, and a printer pressed them in turn. Many copies, so many museums own one.

intro.title: They changed Western art
intro.text: When the prints reached Europe, Monet, Van Gogh and Degas collected them. Flat colour and bold cropping followed.

questions.q: Ukiyo-e means…
questions.explain: A Buddhist idea of fleeting life, recast as city pleasures.

questions.q: Who made The Great Wave?
questions.explain: About 1831.

questions.q: How were ukiyo-e made?
questions.explain: A key block for the outlines, plus one carved block for each colour.

questions.q: What did European artists borrow from Japanese prints?
questions.explain: Called Japonisme. Look at Cassatt and Van Gogh.

questions.q: The Great Wave comes from which series?
options: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
questions.explain: Hokusai, c.1830–32. Red Fuji is from it too.

questions.q: Which Hiroshige print did Van Gogh copy in oil?
questions.explain: In 1887, along with Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge.

edo-japan.look: woodblock prints of actors, beauties and landscapes, with flat colour and strong outlines

vienna-1900.name: Vienna 1900: Klimt

intro.title: Breaking away
intro.text: In 1897 Klimt and friends left Vienna's official art body to found the Vienna Secession. They wanted modern art in every part of life: paintings, posters, furniture and buildings.

intro.title: Gold
intro.text: Klimt's 'golden period' used real gold leaf and patterns borrowed from mosaics: dreamy, sensual figures wrapped in glittering decoration.

intro.title: Record breaker
intro.text: In November 2025 his Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer sold for $236.4m, a record for modern art at auction.

questions.q: The Vienna Secession was founded in…
questions.explain: Klimt was its first president.

questions.q: Where is Klimt's The Kiss?
questions.explain: Bought by the Austrian state in 1908, the year it was first shown. It hangs in the Upper Belvedere.

questions.q: What makes The Kiss shimmer?
questions.explain: From Klimt's 'golden period'.

questions.q: Which Klimt set a record for modern art at auction in 2025?
questions.explain: $236.4m at Sotheby's New York.

questions.q: Which younger Viennese artist did Klimt mentor?
questions.explain: Schiele's twisted, raw figures took Klimt's line in a darker direction.

vienna-1900.look: gold, ornament and psychological intensity, from Klimt to Schiele

fauvism.name: Fauvism

intro.title: Wild beasts
intro.text: At the 1905 Salon d'Automne in Paris, a critic called the painters 'fauves': wild beasts.

intro.title: Colour set free
intro.text: Green faces, red trees, orange skies. Colour expresses feeling, not reality.

intro.title: Who
intro.text: Henri Matisse led, with André Derain and Maurice de Vlaminck. Derain painted the Thames in blazing colour.

questions.q: 'Fauves' means…
questions.explain: The critic Louis Vauxcelles' jibe, 1905.

questions.q: Who led Fauvism?
questions.explain: Matisse; Braque also painted Fauvist works before Cubism.

questions.q: What's the defining feature of a Fauvist painting?
questions.explain: Colour as emotion.

questions.q: Woman with a Hat was shown at…
questions.explain: The show that named the movement.

questions.q: Matisse's Dance (1910) uses just three colours. Which?
questions.explain: Commissioned by the Moscow collector Sergei Shchukin.

questions.q: Which Moscow collector commissioned Matisse's Dance (1910)?
questions.explain: Dance and its partner, Music, were made for his Moscow mansion. Both are now in the Hermitage, St Petersburg.

questions.q: Which Paris dealer sent André Derain to London in 1906 to paint the city?
questions.explain: Derain painted the Thames, its bridges and Westminster in blazing colour.

fauvism.look: wild, unnatural colour used for its own sake

expressionism.name: Expressionism

intro.title: Inside out
intro.text: Painting how the world feels, not how it looks: anxiety, longing, energy.

intro.title: The forerunner
intro.text: Munch's The Scream (1893) came first. Van Gogh's emotional colour mattered too.

intro.title: Two German groups
intro.text: Die Brücke (Dresden, 1905, with Kirchner) and Der Blaue Reiter (Munich, 1911, with Kandinsky and Franz Marc).

questions.q: Expressionism is mainly linked with which country?
questions.explain: Dresden, Berlin and Munich.

questions.q: Who painted The Scream?
questions.explain: Norwegian, 1893. Several versions exist.

questions.q: Expressionist paintings aim to show…
questions.explain: Distortion and clashing colour express feeling.

questions.q: Which is typical of Expressionism?
questions.explain: Tension made visible.

questions.q: Die Brücke was founded in 1905 in…
questions.explain: By architecture students including Kirchner.

questions.q: Der Blaue Reiter was co-founded by Kandinsky and…
questions.explain: Munich, 1911. Marc loved blue horses.

questions.q: Where is the 1893 painted version of The Scream?
questions.explain: The National Museum in Oslo.

expressionism.look: distorted forms and harsh colour that express inner feelings

cubism.name: Cubism

intro.title: Many views at once
intro.text: Picasso and Braque broke objects into facets, showing several sides at the same time.

intro.title: The shock
intro.text: Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) stunned even his friends. Cubism followed.

intro.title: Spreading out
intro.text: Léger's tubes, Picabia's colour, Duchamp's motion: Cubism became a language others bent.

questions.q: Who invented Cubism?
questions.explain: Working side by side in Paris from about 1908.

questions.q: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon is in…
questions.explain: Since 1939.

questions.q: The key idea of Cubism is…
questions.explain: Objects are broken into planes and reassembled.

questions.q: Early (Analytic) Cubist paintings mostly use…
questions.explain: A narrow palette so you focus on form.

questions.q: Gluing paper into a picture, used in Synthetic Cubism, is called…
questions.explain: Braque made the first one in 1912.

questions.q: Why was Léger's Cubism nicknamed 'Tubism'?
questions.explain: Look at Contrast of Forms.

questions.q: Nude Descending a Staircase caused a stir at which 1913 show?
questions.explain: One critic called it 'an explosion in a shingle factory'.

questions.q: The critic who wrote in 1908 that Braque reduced everything to cubes had named which movement in 1905?
questions.explain: Louis Vauxcelles called Matisse's circle 'les fauves', wild beasts, in 1905.

2.title: Many views at once
2.text: Working side by side from about 1908, Picasso and Braque broke objects into facets, as if you could see them from several angles in a single picture.

2.title: Two phases
2.text: Early Cubism used muted browns and greys and took forms apart. From around 1912 it turned brighter and simpler, and artists began gluing paper and other materials onto their pictures, an early kind of collage.

2.title: Cézanne's legacy
2.text: They built on Cézanne's advice to see nature in terms of simple shapes: the cylinder, the sphere and the cone.

cubism.look: objects broken into facets, as if seen from several angles at once

abstraction.name: Abstract art

intro.title: No subject at all
intro.text: Around 1910 artists asked: can colour and shape alone carry meaning, like music?

intro.title: Three pioneers
intro.text: Kandinsky (musical and expressive), Malevich (pure geometry) and Mondrian (grids).

intro.title: De Stijl
intro.text: A Dutch group founded in 1917 by Theo van Doesburg, with Mondrian as its star: straight lines, right angles, black, white, grey and the three primary colours.

questions.q: Abstract art shows…
questions.explain: Colour, line and shape for their own sake.

questions.q: Black Square (1915) was painted by…
questions.explain: First shown in Petrograd (St Petersburg) in 1915, it launched Suprematism.

questions.q: Mondrian's signature style uses…
options: Black grid lines and primary colours
questions.explain: Red, yellow, blue, with black and white.

questions.q: Kandinsky compared painting to…
questions.explain: He gave his paintings musical titles like Compositions and Improvisations.

questions.q: Malevich's movement of pure geometric shapes is called…
questions.explain: Launched in 1915.

questions.q: Broadway Boogie Woogie was inspired by…
questions.explain: Mondrian moved to New York in 1940.

questions.q: De Stijl, Mondrian's group, came from…
questions.explain: Founded in 1917 by Theo van Doesburg, with Mondrian as its star.

questions.q: Malevich showed Black Square in 1915 at an exhibition in Petrograd (St Petersburg) called…
questions.explain: Said 'zero-ten'. The zero is often read as starting painting again from nothing.

abstraction.look: pictures with no recognisable subject, just colour, line and shape

intro.title: Anti-art
intro.text: Born in Zurich in 1916, at the Cabaret Voltaire, in disgust at the First World War. Nonsense as protest.

intro.title: Readymades
intro.text: Marcel Duchamp chose ordinary objects and declared them art. The idea mattered more than the making.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Collage, photomontage, chance, jokes, cut-up words.

questions.q: Dada got its name and started in 1916 at the Cabaret Voltaire in…
questions.explain: The club was founded by Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings. Similar anti-art ideas were brewing in New York at the same time.

questions.q: Dada was a reaction to…
questions.explain: If reason led to war, Dada chose nonsense.

questions.q: A 'readymade' is…
options: An everyday object presented as art
questions.explain: Duchamp's invention.

questions.q: Duchamp's Fountain is a…
questions.explain: Signed 'R. Mutt', 1917. Tate's version is a 1964 replica.

questions.q: What did Duchamp add to the Mona Lisa in L.H.O.O.Q.?
questions.explain: On a cheap postcard, 1919.

questions.q: Duchamp signed Fountain with a made-up name. Which?
questions.explain: 'R. Mutt 1917', in black paint. Rrose Sélavy was a different alter ego Duchamp used later.

questions.q: The original Fountain of 1917 is lost. What is the one at Tate in London?
options: A plaster model made by Tate
questions.explain: Duchamp approved a small edition of replicas in 1964. The original survives only in a photograph by Alfred Stieglitz.

questions.q: In 1917 Fountain was sent to a New York show that promised to hang anything entered. Whose show?
questions.explain: It was never put on display. Duchamp, one of the society's directors, resigned in protest.

questions.q: Which Romanian-born poet wrote the Dada Manifesto of 1918?
questions.explain: Tzara read it in Zurich. It argued for doubt, nonsense and spontaneity.

surrealism.name: Surrealism

intro.title: Dreams on canvas
intro.text: André Breton's 1924 manifesto: free the unconscious mind. Freud's ideas were everywhere.

intro.title: Two routes
intro.text: Precise dream scenes (Dalí, Magritte, and Ernst's Celebes, pictured) or letting the hand wander freely (Miró, and Ernst's later rubbings).

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Melting, floating or misplaced objects, eerie empty spaces, visual puns.

questions.q: Who wrote the Surrealist Manifesto in 1924?
questions.explain: A poet who had trained in medicine.

questions.q: Surrealism explores…
questions.explain: Inspired by Freud.

questions.q: The melting clocks painting is by…
questions.explain: The Persistence of Memory, 1931, at MoMA.

questions.q: Which is most Surrealist?
questions.explain: Dream logic, painted realistically.

questions.q: 'Ceci n'est pas une pipe' is written under a painting by…
questions.explain: The Treachery of Images, 1929.

questions.q: What's on top of Dalí's telephone at Tate in London?
questions.explain: Lobster Telephone, 1938, made with the collector Edward James.

questions.q: Dalí showed Metamorphosis of Narcissus to which visitor in London in 1938?
questions.explain: Freud had just fled Vienna.

questions.q: Who gave a talk in a deep-sea diving suit at the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London?
questions.explain: He nearly ran out of air before the helmet could be taken off.

2.title: Freud and dreams
2.text: The poet André Breton launched Surrealism in Paris in 1924 with a manifesto. Inspired by Freud, the Surrealists wanted to unlock the unconscious mind.

2.title: Two approaches
2.text: Some, like Dalí and Magritte, painted dream scenes in precise, realistic detail. Others, like Miró and Max Ernst, let chance and ‘automatic’ drawing guide the hand.

2.title: Out of Dada
2.text: Many Surrealists began in Dada, the anti-art movement born during the First World War, and kept its love of shock and humour.

surrealism.look: dreamlike scenes and strange combinations drawn from the unconscious

abexp.name: Abstract Expressionism

intro.title: New York takes over
intro.text: After the Second World War, New York painters made huge abstract canvases to express raw feeling, and New York took over from Paris as the centre of the art world.

intro.title: Action painting
intro.text: Pollock laid canvas on the floor and dripped paint: the gesture is the subject.

intro.title: Colour field
intro.text: Rothko made huge glowing blocks of colour to swallow the viewer. Tate has a whole Rothko Room.

questions.q: Abstract Expressionism was centred in…
questions.explain: Pollock, Rothko, de Kooning, Krasner.

questions.q: Pollock's energetic, whole-body way of painting was dubbed…
questions.explain: The critic Harold Rosenberg's term, 1952.

questions.q: Rothko's paintings are…
questions.explain: Meant to be seen up close, in dim light.

questions.q: Rothko's Seagram murals were first meant for…
questions.explain: The Four Seasons in New York. He pulled out and later gave nine to Tate.

questions.q: When did Rothko's murals arrive at Tate in London?
questions.explain: They arrived on 25 February 1970, the day he was found dead.

abexp.look: huge abstract canvases of energetic brushwork or fields of colour, made in New York

popart.name: Pop Art

intro.title: Born in Britain
intro.text: Art made from adverts, comics and celebrity. It began in London: Richard Hamilton's 1956 collage is often called the first Pop artwork. Pictured: David Hockney's A Bigger Splash, 1967.

intro.title: Then America
intro.text: Warhol's soup cans and Marilyns, Lichtenstein's comic-strip panels with Ben-Day dots.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Adverts, celebrities, comics, packaging. Flat bright colour, repetition, screenprinting.

questions.q: Pop Art took its imagery from…
questions.explain: Popular culture.

questions.q: Who made Campbell's Soup Cans?
questions.explain: 32 canvases, 1962. At MoMA.

questions.q: Lichtenstein copied printing dots from comics. They're called…
questions.explain: After the illustrator Benjamin Day.

questions.q: Warhol's favourite technique for repeating images was…
questions.explain: Fast, mechanical, endlessly repeatable.

questions.q: Whaam! (Tate, London) is based on…
questions.explain: A 1962 panel from All-American Men of War.

questions.q: Where was David Hockney born?
questions.explain: In 1937. He moved to LA in the 1960s.

questions.q: Marilyn Diptych was made…
questions.explain: In 1962. Colour on the left, fading black and white on the right.

2.title: Britain first
2.text: Pop Art began in Britain. In the 1950s London's Independent Group, including Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi, were fascinated by American adverts, comics and films. Later British artists like David Hockney took up its bright, flat look; he painted this Californian pool in 1967.

2.title: New York
2.text: In the early 1960s Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein borrowed from soup cans, comic strips and celebrity photos. Warhol used commercial silkscreen printing, while Lichtenstein copied the dots of cheap printing by hand.

2.title: Why it mattered
2.text: Pop blurred the line between ‘high’ art and everyday mass culture, and asked whether art could be made like any other product.

popart.look: bright imagery borrowed from adverts, comics and celebrity

modern-british.name: Modern British art

intro.title: A British century
intro.text: Not one style but a century of British artists making modern art their own, often rooted in place: Paul Nash's war landscapes, L.S. Lowry's northern streets, Barbara Hepworth's carvings from St Ives.

intro.title: Carving
intro.text: Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth made British sculpture world-famous.

intro.title: School of London
intro.text: Bacon and Freud, friends and rivals, painted the body with raw intensity.

questions.q: Which sculptor lived and worked in St Ives, Cornwall?
questions.explain: Her studio and garden there are run by Tate.

questions.q: L.S. Lowry painted the industrial streets of…
questions.explain: Famous for crowds of 'matchstick' figures.

questions.q: Bridget Riley's black-and-white paintings belong to…
questions.explain: Optical art: patterns that seem to move.

questions.q: Francis Bacon's figures are usually…
questions.explain: Raw and unsettling.

questions.q: Stanley Spencer set The Resurrection in…
questions.explain: The dead rise from Cookham churchyard, Berkshire.

questions.q: Totes Meer (Dead Sea) by Paul Nash shows…
questions.explain: A sea of broken planes, painted in 1940–41.

questions.q: Paula Rego grew up in…
questions.explain: Born in Lisbon, she settled in London.

modern-british.look: British painting and sculpture of the 20th century, from figurative to abstract

yba.name: Young British Artists

intro.title: Freeze, 1988
intro.text: A loud, shocking generation of London artists in the 1990s. It began when student Damien Hirst organised a show called Freeze in an empty Docklands building.

intro.title: The patron
intro.text: Adman Charles Saatchi bought heavily. His 'Sensation' show at the Royal Academy (1997) caused uproar.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Shock, everyday materials, death, confession: sharks in formaldehyde, unmade beds, casts of empty spaces.

questions.q: Which show launched the YBAs in 1988?
questions.explain: Organised by Hirst. Frieze, the fair, came later (2003).

questions.q: Who was the YBAs' big collector?
questions.explain: His 'Sensation' show went to the RA in 1997.

questions.q: YBA art often used…
questions.explain: Animals, beds, medicine cabinets.

questions.q: My Bed is a work by…
questions.explain: Shown at the Turner Prize in 1999.

questions.q: Pharmacy (Tate, London) was also the name of Hirst's…
questions.explain: A real restaurant in Notting Hill, opened in the late 1990s.

yba.look: shock, wit and everyday materials, from 1990s London

bloomsbury.name: Bloomsbury: Bell & Grant

intro.title: Who were they?
intro.text: Two painters at the heart of the Bloomsbury Group, a circle of London artists, writers and thinkers that included Vanessa's sister, Virginia Woolf. Bell and Grant lived and worked together for over 40 years.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: Tate Britain's 'Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury' runs 12 November 2026 to 11 April 2027.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Bold colour and simple shapes inspired by French painters like Cézanne and Matisse, still daring in Britain then. They also decorated furniture, fabrics and pottery, and painted almost every surface of Charleston, their Sussex farmhouse.

questions.q: Vanessa Bell's sister was…
questions.explain: The novelist.

questions.q: The Bloomsbury Group is named after…
questions.explain: Where many of them lived, around Gordon Square.

questions.q: Bell and Grant's bold colour came from seeing…
questions.explain: Roger Fry's 1910 and 1912 London shows changed their painting.

questions.q: Bloomsbury artists also designed…
questions.explain: Through Roger Fry's Omega Workshops.

questions.q: Bell and Grant's painted home in Sussex is…
questions.explain: Now open to visitors.

questions.q: Roger Fry's design company (1913) was the…
questions.explain: In Fitzroy Square. (The Hogarth Press was the Woolfs' publishing house.)

questions.q: Studland Beach (Tate, London) was painted by…
questions.explain: In 1912, simplifying figures into blocks of colour.

bloomsbury.look: bold colour and pattern, influenced by Post-Impressionism

intro.title: Who was she?
intro.text: An American heiress (1898–1979) who became one of the boldest collectors of modern art, buying Surrealist and abstract works when few others would. Her Venice palazzo is now her museum.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: 'Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector' at the Royal Academy, 21 November 2026 to 14 March 2027.

intro.title: Cork Street to New York
intro.text: Her first gallery, Guggenheim Jeune, ran at 30 Cork Street, London, in 1938–39 and gave Kandinsky his first UK solo show. Later, in New York, she championed a young Jackson Pollock.

questions.q: Peggy Guggenheim was famous as a…
questions.explain: One of the 20th century's great collectors.

questions.q: Her London gallery was called…
questions.explain: A pun on the Paris gallery Bernheim-Jeune.

questions.q: Her collection is strongest in…
questions.explain: She was briefly married to the Surrealist Max Ernst.

questions.q: Which young American did she champion in New York?
questions.explain: She gave him a contract and his first solo show (1943).

questions.q: Where is her collection now?
questions.explain: Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, on the Grand Canal.

questions.q: Peggy Guggenheim was briefly married to which Surrealist painter?
questions.explain: They married in 1941 and split up a few years later.

questions.q: What was her New York gallery, opened in 1942, called?
questions.explain: It showed Surrealist and abstract art, and gave Jackson Pollock his first solo show.

questions.q: Her museum in Venice is an unfinished 18th-century palace on the Grand Canal. What's it called?
questions.explain: She bought it in 1949. Only the ground floor was ever built.

intro.title: Sugar money
intro.text: Sugar refiner Henry Tate funded the first gallery at Millbank, opened 1897. Now Tate Britain.

intro.title: Four Tates
intro.text: Tate Britain and Tate Modern in London, plus Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives.

intro.title: Turner Prize
intro.text: Set up in 1984, named after J.M.W. Turner, who left his work to the nation.

questions.q: Tate Modern is in a former…
questions.explain: Bankside Power Station, converted by Herzog & de Meuron, opened 2000.

questions.q: Henry Tate made his fortune from…
questions.explain: Tate & Lyle descends from his company.

questions.q: Which Tate shows British art from 1500 to now?
questions.explain: At Millbank, by the Thames.

questions.q: The Turner Prize began in…
questions.explain: Malcolm Morley was the first winner.

questions.q: Tate Britain's Clore Gallery holds…
questions.explain: Turner left around 300 oils and thousands of drawings to the nation.

intro.title: Founded 1824
intro.text: It began with 38 paintings from the collection of the late financier John Julius Angerstein, bought by the government in 1824. It moved to Trafalgar Square in 1838.

intro.title: Free for all
intro.text: Western European painting from about 1250 to 1900, free to enter.

intro.title: Star pictures
intro.text: The Arnolfini Portrait, The Ambassadors, The Hay Wain, The Fighting Temeraire, Sunflowers.

questions.q: London's National Gallery is on…
questions.explain: Since 1838.

questions.q: London's National Gallery was founded in…
questions.explain: The British Museum is older (1753).

questions.q: London's National Gallery collection stops at about…
questions.explain: Later art is mostly at Tate.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT at the National Gallery in London?
questions.explain: Millais' Ophelia is at Tate Britain.

questions.q: The founding collection came from which financier?
questions.explain: 38 paintings from his collection, bought by the government in 1824 after his death.

intro.title: Run by artists
intro.text: Founded by George III in 1768. Elected artists put 'RA' after their names.

intro.title: Summer Exhibition
intro.text: Every year since 1769: the world's oldest open-submission show. Anyone can enter.

intro.title: On now
intro.text: Painting the French Riviera runs until 31 January 2027, and Peggy Guggenheim in London until 14 March 2027.

questions.q: The Royal Academy is on…
questions.explain: Burlington House.

questions.q: Who founded the Royal Academy in 1768?
questions.explain: Reynolds was its first President.

questions.q: What's special about the Summer Exhibition?
questions.explain: Held every year since 1769.

questions.q: Which controversial YBA show did the RA host in 1997?
questions.explain: Charles Saatchi's collection.

intro.title: The big two
intro.text: Sotheby's (1744) and Christie's (1766), both founded in London. Phillips is the third big name.

intro.title: How a sale works
intro.text: Each lot has an estimate. The hammer price is the winning bid; the buyer then pays a premium on top.

intro.title: Records
intro.text: Salvator Mundi made $450.3m in 2017. Klimt's Lederer portrait made $236.4m in 2025.

questions.q: Which of these auction houses is the oldest?
questions.explain: Sotheby's, 1744. Christie's followed in 1766.

questions.q: The most expensive painting ever sold at auction is…
questions.explain: $450.3m, Christie's New York, 2017.

questions.q: The extra fee a buyer pays on top of the hammer price is the…
questions.explain: A percentage of the hammer price.

questions.q: The secret minimum price a seller will accept is the…
questions.explain: If bidding falls short, the lot is 'bought in'.

questions.q: When an auction house gives a seller a 'guarantee', it means…
options: The seller is promised a minimum price
The lot is sold without a reserve
questions.explain: Houses offer it to win big consignments.

questions.q: Interchange by de Kooning reportedly sold privately in 2015 for about…
questions.explain: One of the highest prices ever paid for a painting.

intro.title: Shopping malls for art
intro.text: Hundreds of galleries rent booths for a few days. Much of the year's selling happens here.

intro.title: Art Basel
intro.text: Founded in Basel in 1970. Now also in Miami Beach, Hong Kong, Paris (in the Grand Palais) and, since 2026, Doha in Qatar.

intro.title: Frieze
intro.text: Frieze London launched in Regent's Park in 2003. Frieze Masters, for older art, followed in 2012.

questions.q: Art Basel was founded in…
questions.explain: By Basel gallerists including Ernst Beyeler.

questions.q: Frieze London takes place in…
questions.explain: Every October.

questions.q: At an art fair, who sells the art?
questions.explain: Each gallery rents a booth.

questions.q: Where is Art Basel Paris held?
questions.explain: The restored Grand Palais.

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Lahore, Pakistan, in 1983, he trained in the US and lives in New York. A 2020 solo show at the Whitney Museum made his name.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: 'Salman Toor: Someone Like You' at the Courtauld Gallery, London, runs until 10 January 2027. It's his first solo museum show in Europe: 19 paintings.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Friends in bars, cabs and bedrooms, painted from memory with loose, sketchy brushwork. A glowing green comes back again and again.

questions.q: Where was Salman Toor born?
questions.explain: In 1983. He now lives and works in New York.

questions.q: Which colour fills many of Toor's paintings?
questions.explain: A glowing green, almost like absinthe, sets the mood in many of his scenes.

questions.q: Where is 'Salman Toor: Someone Like You' on until 10 January 2027?
questions.explain: It's his first solo museum show in Europe.

questions.q: Which famous painting does The Bar on East 13th rework?
options: Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
Renoir's Luncheon of the Boating Party
Van Gogh's Café Terrace at Night
questions.explain: Manet's 1882 bar scene belongs to the Courtauld, so the two hang under the same roof during the show.

questions.q: Where does Toor live and work?
questions.explain: He trained in the US, at Ohio Wesleyan University and then Pratt Institute in Brooklyn.

questions.q: Who are the people in his paintings?
options: Imagined figures, drawn from his own life and friends
questions.explain: The scenes draw on his own life and memories, but the figures are largely imagined rather than portraits.

questions.q: Which New York museum gave Toor his breakthrough solo show in 2020?
options: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
Museum of Modern Art, New York
Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
questions.explain: 'How Will I Know' ran at the Whitney in 2020 to 2021.

questions.q: In 2021 the Frick Collection in New York hung his painting Museum Boys next to works by…
questions.explain: Two Vermeers: a sign of how closely his work talks to the Old Masters.

questions.q: Which kind of older painting does Toor admire most?
questions.explain: He has named Van Dyck, Rubens, Caravaggio and Watteau among his influences.

questions.q: Toor calls his 2019 paintings, like Bar Boy, his…
questions.explain: From 2019 he began to paint his own life, including being gay, much more openly.

questions.q: Which big international exhibition included Toor in 2024?
questions.explain: He was in the main exhibition of the 60th Venice Biennale.

questions.q: For the Courtauld show he made a new painting modelled on a Renaissance work in its collection. Which?
questions.explain: Lotto painted it in the 1550s. Toor's new picture borrows its composition.

questions.q: Toor illustrated Jungle Nama (2021), a story in verse by which writer?
questions.explain: A retelling of a legend from the Sundarbans, the mangrove forests of India and Bangladesh.

van-gogh.name: Vincent van Gogh

intro.title: Who was he?
intro.text: A Dutch painter (1853–1890) who poured his feelings into colour and brushwork. He painted for only about ten years and sold very little, but became one of the best-loved artists of all.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: On 18 November 2026 Sotheby's in New York offers Blossoming Chestnut Trees, one of his last paintings from 1890, estimated at about $180m.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Thick paint you can almost feel, swirling brushstrokes and bold, bright colour. Japanese prints taught him strong outlines and flat areas of colour.

questions.q: In which country was Van Gogh born?
questions.explain: In 1853, in Zundert, a village in the south of the Netherlands.

questions.q: Which museum has the world's largest collection of Van Gogh's work?
options: Museum of Modern Art, New York
questions.explain: It grew from the family's own collection and opened in 1973.

questions.q: Which brother, an art dealer in Paris, supported Vincent with money for years?
questions.explain: Theo paid for his paints and living costs, and the two wrote hundreds of letters to each other.

questions.q: In February 1888 Van Gogh left Paris and moved to…
questions.explain: He rented rooms in the Yellow House and painted some of his best-known works there.

questions.q: Which painter came to stay with him in Arles in late 1888?
questions.explain: Gauguin stayed about two months. Van Gogh had painted Sunflowers that August to decorate the room Gauguin would use.

questions.q: Which 1885 painting shows a peasant family eating supper by lamplight?
questions.explain: Painted in Nuenen in the Netherlands, in dark earthy colours, before Paris brightened his palette.

questions.q: Van Gogh collected cheap woodblock prints from which country?
questions.explain: He even made painted copies of some, such as Hiroshige's Plum Park in Kameido.

questions.q: Where did Van Gogh paint The Starry Night in 1889?
options: In a hospital at Saint-Rémy, Provence
In his brother's flat in Paris
In the Yellow House in Arles
questions.explain: He had gone there to recover. The view is from his window, but the village was largely invented.

questions.q: Which painting is usually said to be the only one Van Gogh sold in his lifetime?
questions.explain: The Belgian painter Anna Boch bought it in 1890 for about 400 francs. Records suggest he sold at least one other work too. It's now in the Pushkin Museum, Moscow.

questions.q: Van Gogh painted Almond Blossom (1890) as a gift. What was it celebrating?
options: The birth of his brother Theo's son
questions.explain: The baby was named Vincent Willem after him. Years later that nephew founded the Van Gogh Museum.

questions.q: Which three of these did Van Gogh paint while living in Arles?
questions.explain: Sunflowers, Café Terrace at Night and The Yellow House all date from 1888 in Arles. The Starry Night and the Wheatfield come from Saint-Rémy (1889), The Potato Eaters from Nuenen (1885).

questions.q: Who did most to make Van Gogh famous after he and Theo died?
questions.explain: She looked after hundreds of his paintings and drawings, lent them to exhibitions and published his letters to Theo in 1914.

questions.q: The National Gallery in London has the finished A Wheatfield, with Cypresses. Where is his first version, painted outdoors?
options: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
questions.explain: He painted it in June 1889 near Saint-Rémy and saw it as a study for the London picture.

2.title: A late start
2.text: Van Gogh worked as an art dealer, a teacher and a preacher before deciding, at 27, to become an artist. His early pictures, like The Potato Eaters, are dark and earthy.

2.title: Paris and colour
2.text: In Paris, from 1886 to 1888, he met the Impressionists and fell for Japanese prints, and his colours brightened dramatically. The love of Japan stayed with him: a Japanese print hangs behind him in this self-portrait, painted in Arles in 1889.

2.title: The last years
2.text: In Arles in the south of France he painted his Sunflowers. After a breakdown he spent a year at an asylum in Saint-Rémy, where he painted The Starry Night. He died in Auvers in 1890.

van-gogh.look: bold colour and simplified forms, with each artist going their own way

alfred-wallis.name: Alfred Wallis

intro.title: Who was he?
intro.text: A sailor and fisherman, born in Devon, who settled in St Ives, Cornwall, and later dealt in scrap from ships. He began painting at about 70, after his wife died, with no training at all.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: 'Alfred Wallis: an Artists' Artist' opens at Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, on 21 November 2026 and runs until May 2027.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Boats, harbours and lighthouses painted from memory on scraps of cardboard, often with ship's paint. No perspective: important things are simply bigger.

questions.q: At about what age did Alfred Wallis start painting?
questions.explain: Around 1925, a few years after his wife died.

questions.q: Wallis lived and painted in which seaside town?
questions.explain: His family moved there in 1882. His grave looks down over the town and Tate St Ives.

questions.q: What did Wallis usually paint on?
questions.explain: Often torn from boxes, odd shapes and all. He used household and ship's paint.

questions.q: What did Wallis mostly paint?
questions.explain: Above all the sailing ships he had known as a young man.

questions.q: Which two of these artists came across Wallis on a day trip to St Ives in 1928 and bought his paintings?
questions.explain: Ben Nicholson and Christopher Wood spotted his paintings in August 1928 and soon introduced his work to other artists.

questions.q: Wallis painted his boats and harbours mostly…
questions.explain: Often the sailing ships of his youth, by then being replaced by motor boats.

questions.q: Wallis had no art training. Art by self-taught painters like him is often called…
questions.explain: 'Naive' here means untrained, not foolish: direct, simple and often very bold.

questions.q: In Wallis's pictures, what usually decides how big something is?
questions.explain: He ignored perspective, so his harbours often look like old maps.

questions.q: Which collector, whose home Kettle's Yard in Cambridge is now a museum, championed Wallis?
questions.explain: Ede promoted Wallis in London. Kettle's Yard still shows his paintings.

questions.q: Which famous potter made the tiles on Wallis's grave in St Ives?
questions.explain: They show a small old man at the foot of a lighthouse, a subject Wallis often painted.

questions.q: Wallis painted Voyage to Labrador from memories of his years at sea. Labrador is part of which country today?
questions.explain: As a young sailor he crossed the Atlantic on schooners and spent months there as ship's cook.

questions.q: Boats at Quayside was begun by one artist and finished by Wallis. Who started it?
questions.explain: Wood began this view of a harbour in Brittany and probably gave it to Wallis around 1930, who completed it.

questions.q: Why did Wallis say he took up painting?
questions.explain: He told Ben Nicholson so after his wife's death. His pictures sold for only a few shillings.

alfred-wallis.look: British painting and sculpture of the 20th century, from figurative to abstract

capitalist-realism.name: Capitalist Realism
capitalist-realism.look: blurry paintings copied from newspaper photos and adverts, Germany's sceptical answer to pop art

intro.title: Düsseldorf, 1963
intro.text: Young painters in West Germany, including Gerhard Richter, Sigmar Polke and Konrad Lueg, launched a movement to challenge the dominance of American pop art.

intro.title: A jokey name
intro.text: The label mocks Socialist Realism, the official art of the Soviet bloc, while also poking at Western consumer culture. Cold War Germany sat right between the two.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Everyday images borrowed from magazines, snapshots and adverts, often in grey, and often blurred so they look like a photo slightly out of focus.

questions.q: Which art did Capitalist Realism set out to challenge?
questions.explain: Tate describes it as a German response to the dominance of American pop art in the West.

questions.q: Which official Soviet style does the name Capitalist Realism mock?
questions.explain: Socialist Realism was the state-approved art of the Soviet Union, so the name is a Cold War joke.

questions.q: Where did Richter and Konrad Lueg stage Living with Pop in 1963?
questions.explain: The event, subtitled A Demonstration for Capitalist Realism, took place in the Berges furniture store.

questions.q: Which painter was a founding Capitalist Realist alongside Richter?
questions.explain: Polke and Richter were fellow students at the Düsseldorf Art Academy, and first showed together in 1963.

black-figuration.name: Black figuration
black-figuration.look: Black figures painted at the centre of the grand traditions of Western painting
black-figuration.as: by a painter of Black figuration

intro.title: Who gets painted?
intro.text: For centuries Western painting mostly showed white people. Black figuration puts Black people at the heart of the picture, as heroes, lovers, painters and dreamers.

intro.title: A new generation
intro.text: Kerry James Marshall has painted Black figures since 1980. Younger painters such as Lynette Yiadom-Boakye, Amy Sherald and Kehinde Wiley are part of the same wave.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Black figures at full size, in poses borrowed from Old Master portraits, history paintings and Rococo scenes, but painted on their own terms.

questions.q: What do Black figuration painters put at the centre of their pictures?
questions.explain: They paint Black people in formats long dominated by white sitters and white artists.

questions.q: Which painter made his first painting of a Black figure in 1980?
questions.explain: It was Portrait of the Artist as a Shadow of His Former Self, a small egg tempera painting.

questions.q: Lynette Yiadom-Boakye is known for painting…
questions.explain: Her figures are invented, drawn from scrapbooks, memory and imagination rather than real sitters.

questions.q: Which older style does Marshall borrow in his Vignette paintings?
questions.explain: He used the airy, romantic look of 18th-century French Rococo to paint Black love.

british-black-arts.name: British Black Arts Movement
british-black-arts.look: bold, political art by young Black British artists about race, gender and history
british-black-arts.as: by a British Black Arts artist

intro.title: Wolverhampton, 1982
intro.text: The movement began with the First National Black Art Convention, organised by the Blk Art Group at Wolverhampton Polytechnic.

intro.title: Why it mattered
intro.text: Young Black and Asian artists in Britain were largely shut out of galleries. Inspired by thinkers like Stuart Hall, they used art to question race, gender and Britain's imperial past.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Strong colour, cut-outs, collage, film and text. Black people shown as the main characters of history, not on its edges.

questions.q: In which city did the 1982 First National Black Art Convention happen?
questions.explain: It was organised by the Blk Art Group at Wolverhampton Polytechnic.

questions.q: Which 1989 Hayward Gallery show brought these artists to wide attention?
questions.explain: Curated by Rasheed Araeen, it showed artists of African, Caribbean and Asian descent working in Britain.

questions.q: Which thinker inspired and championed the movement?
questions.explain: The cultural theorist wrote about race and how the media represent people.

questions.q: Which artist organised Five Black Women at London's Africa Centre in 1983?
questions.explain: Himid curated several shows in the 1980s to challenge the invisibility of Black women artists.

installation-art.name: Installation art
installation-art.look: whole rooms you walk into, made of light, mirrors, sound and everyday things

intro.title: Step inside
intro.text: Instead of a picture on a wall, the artwork is a whole space you walk into. It grew from 'environments' of the late 1950s and became a major strand of art from the 1960s.

intro.title: The Turbine Hall
intro.text: Tate Modern's vast Turbine Hall hosts a big new commission most years. A glowing sun, a crack in the floor, a sea of porcelain seeds and a fountain have all appeared there.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Rooms of mirrors and light, mist and sound, or piles of everyday things: seeds, shoes, furniture, bottle tops. Often made for one place, and sometimes only for a few months.

questions.q: What does installation art usually invite you to do?
options: Walk into it and experience the space
Look at it in a gold frame
questions.explain: Installations often fill a whole room, and the viewer's experience is a central part of the work.

questions.q: Which London space hosts a huge new installation most years?
questions.explain: Its commissions have included Eliasson's sun, Salcedo's crack, Ai Weiwei's seeds and Kara Walker's fountain.

questions.q: From which decade did installation art become a major strand of art?
questions.explain: It grew even more prominent in the early 1990s.

questions.q: Which American artist began making walk-in 'environments' around 1957?
questions.explain: Tate traces installation art back to Kaprow's environments, with Kurt Schwitters's Merzbau as an earlier forerunner.

afrofuturism.name: Afrofuturism
afrofuturism.look: science fiction, history and myth imagining new Black futures

intro.title: Past meets future
intro.text: Afrofuturism mixes science fiction, history and fantasy to explore Black experience and reconnect the African diaspora with lost ancestry.

intro.title: Where the name came from
intro.text: Critic Mark Dery coined the term in a 1993 essay. Musicians like Sun Ra and writers like Octavia Butler had already been imagining Black futures.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Hybrid bodies, cosmic or mythic beings, African symbols placed in sci-fi worlds, and imagined futures in place of painful histories.

questions.q: Which genre does Afrofuturism blend with history and fantasy?
questions.explain: Tate describes it as a mix of science fiction, history and fantasy.

questions.q: Who coined the word Afrofuturism in 1993?
questions.explain: Dery used it in his 1993 essay 'Black to the Future'.

questions.q: Which jazz musician built a cosmic, Egyptian-inspired persona?
questions.explain: Tate names him as a key Afrofuturist figure.

questions.q: Which Afrofuturist sculptures were the first contemporary works on the Met's facade?
questions.explain: Mutu's four bronzes filled the empty niches in 2019.

pictures-generation.name: The Pictures Generation
pictures-generation.look: borrowed images from films, ads and magazines, restaged and questioned

intro.title: Pictures, 1977
intro.text: The name comes from 'Pictures', a 1977 show at Artists Space in New York, curated by critic Douglas Crimp. Recognisable images were back.

intro.title: Raised on TV
intro.text: These young New York artists grew up on movies, adverts and magazines. They borrowed those images to ask how pictures shape who we think we are.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Rephotographed ads, staged scenes that look like film stills, and copies of famous images. Mostly photography, but also painting, film and performance.

questions.q: Which city was home to the Pictures Generation?
questions.explain: Its artists gathered in New York in the 1970s, and the Met's 2009 survey covered 1974 to 1984.

questions.q: Which 1977 show gave the Pictures Generation its name?
questions.explain: Douglas Crimp curated it at Artists Space, a non-profit venue in New York.

questions.q: What did these artists mainly borrow from?
questions.explain: They appropriated images from mass media to question them.

questions.q: Which art style were they reacting against?
questions.explain: The Met says they turned back to recognisable images after Minimal and Conceptual Art.

performance-art.name: Performance art
performance-art.look: live actions where the artist's own body is the material

intro.title: Art as action
intro.text: Performance art is made through actions by the artist or others, live or recorded. Often the artist's own body is the medium.

intro.title: Roots and rise
intro.text: Its roots go back to Futurist shows and Dada cabarets of the 1910s, but the term 'performance art' caught on in the 1970s.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Since the live moment passes, museums keep photographs, videos, objects and texts. Look for endurance, risk, repetition and the audience taking part.

questions.q: In performance art, what is often the artist's main material?
questions.explain: Tate describes performance art as using the artist's own body as the medium.

questions.q: In which decade did 'performance art' become a widely used term?
questions.explain: Tate notes the term spread in the 1970s, though its roots go back to the 1910s.

questions.q: Which early movement held wild cabaret evenings in Zurich?
questions.explain: Dada cabarets of the 1910s are often seen as forerunners of performance.

questions.q: How do museums usually collect a live performance?
options: Through photos, video, objects and texts
Only as oil paintings of the event
questions.explain: Tate's Abramović works are sets of photographs and a five-screen video.

video-art.name: Video art
video-art.look: moving images on screens and projections, made for the gallery

intro.title: Moving pictures
intro.text: Video art relies on moving images and sound. It arrived in the 1960s, when cheap video cameras let artists record work outside the gallery.

intro.title: From TV sets to big screens
intro.text: Nam June Paik built sculptures from TV sets. Later artists projected work onto whole walls, often on several screens at once.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Projections in dark rooms, monitors and multiple screens. Many works loop with no beginning or end, so you can walk in at any time.

questions.q: In which decade did video art begin?
questions.explain: Tate says video's arrival in the 1960s changed the course of art.

questions.q: Which artist made sculptures out of TV sets?
questions.explain: Britannica credits Paik with early multi-TV installations.

questions.q: Why did cheap video appeal to 1960s artists?
options: They could record work outside the gallery
It was the only way to sell art
questions.explain: Tate notes video freed artists from relying on the gallery.

questions.q: How is much video art shown today?
questions.explain: Projection allowed large, multi-screen installations, as with Bill Viola.

superflat.name: Superflat
superflat.look: flat colour, bold outlines and cute anime-style characters

intro.title: Murakami's idea
intro.text: Takashi Murakami named Superflat in 2000. He linked the flatness of old Japanese painting to the anime and manga of postwar Japan.

intro.title: Flat in two ways
intro.text: 'Flat' means no depth in the picture, but also the shallowness of consumer culture. Superflat blurs high art, cartoons and merchandise.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Bright flat colour, strong outlines, no perspective, and cute (kawaii) characters, sometimes hiding darker themes like war and the atomic bomb.

questions.q: Which artist named and led Superflat?
questions.explain: He set out his theory in a 2000 essay and show.

questions.q: Which popular art forms shaped Superflat?
questions.explain: Murakami tied Superflat to postwar Japanese animation and comics.

questions.q: Which older Japanese art also has a 'flat' look?
questions.explain: Murakami traced Superflat back to Edo artists such as Ito Jakuchu and Soga Shohaku: bold outlines, flat colour, little perspective.

questions.q: Which US museum showed Superflat in 2001?
questions.explain: It opened at MOCA Pacific Design Center, then toured to Minneapolis and Seattle.

gerhard-richter.name: Gerhard Richter

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Dresden in 1932, he fled East Germany in 1961, just before the Berlin Wall went up. He has lived in Cologne since 1983. His paintings have set auction records.

intro.title: Part of Capitalist Realism
intro.text: In 1963 he and fellow Düsseldorf students coined this tongue-in-cheek label: a German answer to American pop art, made in a country split by the Cold War.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Grey, blurred paintings copied from snapshots and magazines, as if out of focus. Later, huge colourful abstracts scraped with a squeegee.

questions.q: In which city was Gerhard Richter born?
questions.explain: Born in 1932, he trained at the Dresden Academy before fleeing to the West in 1961.

questions.q: What tool does Richter drag across his abstract paintings?
questions.explain: From the mid-1980s he used a homemade squeegee to smear and scrape bands of paint.

questions.q: How does Richter blur his photo paintings?
options: He drags a dry brush through wet paint
questions.explain: Dragging a dry brush through the wet pigment softens every edge.

questions.q: Richter's Mouth (1963) is based on a photo of which actress?
questions.explain: It is one of his earliest surviving canvases.

questions.q: Which cathedral has a huge stained-glass window designed by Richter?
questions.explain: Unveiled in 2007 in the south transept, it is made of 11,263 squares of coloured glass.

gerhard-richter.look: blurred paintings of photos, and big squeegeed abstracts

kerry-james-marshall.name: Kerry James Marshall

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1955, he grew up in Los Angeles near the Black Panthers' headquarters and built his career in Chicago. His 2016 retrospective, Mastry, travelled to the Met Breuer in New York.

intro.title: Part of Black figuration
intro.text: Marshall set out to put Black people into the grand story of Western painting, from which they had long been missing. His first Black figure came in 1980.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Figures painted a deep, pure black, in busy, colourful scenes of gardens, homes and studios. Banners, words and symbols float in the air.

questions.q: What colour does Marshall paint his figures' skin?
questions.explain: The extremely dark skin is his signature, a way of making Blackness impossible to overlook.

questions.q: In which US city has Marshall spent much of his career?
questions.explain: He taught at the University of Illinois in Chicago from 1993 to 2006.

questions.q: What kind of place does Many Mansions show?
questions.explain: It shows Stateway Gardens, a housing project whose cheerful name hid a hard reality.

questions.q: Which painter mentored the young Marshall?
questions.explain: Marshall first saw a real artist's studio when he visited White's as a schoolboy.

questions.q: Which London venue held The Histories, his big 2025 survey?
questions.explain: Running from September 2025 to January 2026, it was his largest show ever in Europe.

kerry-james-marshall.look: grand scenes of Black everyday life, with figures painted a deep, pure black

julie-mehretu.name: Julie Mehretu

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in 1970, she moved to Michigan aged six when her family fled turmoil. She lives in Harlem, New York. In 2021 the Whitney gave her a retrospective.

intro.title: Part of Abstract art
intro.text: Her huge canvases have no clear subject, yet they grow from real places: city plans, stadiums and squares where history was made, buried under storms of marks.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Fine architectural lines and maps in layers, crossed by swarms of inky dashes, swirls and blurred shapes, often on canvases several metres wide.

questions.q: In which city was Julie Mehretu born?
questions.explain: Her family left for Michigan in 1977, where her father taught geography.

questions.q: What does Mehretu layer beneath her swirling marks?
questions.explain: City grids, building plans and charts give her abstract storms a hidden structure.

questions.q: Mogamma is named after a building on which square?
questions.explain: The square was the heart of Egypt's 2011 uprising.

questions.q: Her Goldman Sachs lobby painting, commissioned in 2007, is roughly the size of…
questions.explain: The bank paid $5 million for the commission, simply called Mural.

questions.q: Besides stadium outlines, what fills Stadia II?
questions.explain: The series looks at stadiums as places of spectacle, made as the US drummed up support for the Iraq War.

julie-mehretu.look: huge layered canvases of architectural lines and swirling marks

lynette-yiadom-boakye.name: Lynette Yiadom-Boakye

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in London in 1977 to Ghanaian parents who worked as NHS nurses, she still lives and works in London. She was shortlisted for the Turner Prize in 2013.

intro.title: Part of Black figuration
intro.text: Her paintings helped bring about a revival in painting the Black figure. Tate Britain gave her a major survey, Fly In League With The Night, in 2020.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Relaxed figures reading, resting or lounging against dark, muted backgrounds with no clear time or place. Loose, quick brushwork, and almost never any shoes.

questions.q: Who are the people in Yiadom-Boakye's paintings?
questions.explain: She builds them from scrapbooks, found images and imagination, never live sitters.

questions.q: How long does she usually take to paint one picture?
questions.explain: Finishing in one session gives her paintings their fresh, spontaneous feel.

questions.q: What does she usually leave out to keep figures timeless?
questions.explain: Footwear dates a picture quickly, so her people stay outside any decade.

questions.q: What else does Yiadom-Boakye create besides paintings?
questions.explain: She says she writes the things she doesn't paint, and paints the things she doesn't write.

questions.q: Which award did she win at the 2018 Carnegie International?
questions.explain: She made 13 new paintings for the Pittsburgh show.

lynette-yiadom-boakye.look: portraits of imagined Black figures in dark, loosely painted settings

chris-ofili.name: Chris Ofili

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Manchester in 1968 to Nigerian parents, he studied in London and has lived in Trinidad since 2005. He won the Turner Prize in 1998.

intro.title: Part of the YBAs
intro.text: Charles Saatchi's Sensation show in 1997 launched him with the Young British Artists. His painting of a Black Madonna caused uproar when it toured to New York.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Glittering layers of resin, map pins, collage and dots. Many 1990s canvases lean on two lumps of varnished elephant dung instead of hanging on the wall.

questions.q: Which unusual material made Ofili's 1990s paintings famous?
questions.explain: He began using it after a 1992 trip to Zimbabwe.

questions.q: Which prize did Ofili win in 1998?
