questions.explain: He was the first painter to win it since Howard Hodgkin in 1985.

questions.q: No Woman, No Cry is a tribute to which murdered young man?
questions.explain: It shows his mother Doreen weeping, with tiny pictures of Stephen inside her tears.

questions.q: How many monkey paintings line Ofili's The Upper Room?
questions.explain: Thirteen, like Jesus and the disciples at the Last Supper.

questions.q: Which New York mayor attacked Ofili's The Holy Virgin Mary in 1999?
questions.explain: He fought the Brooklyn Museum over the Sensation show. The painting now belongs to MoMA.

chris-ofili.look: glittering, layered paintings, some propped on balls of elephant dung

lubaina-himid.name: Lubaina Himid

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in Zanzibar in 1954, she came to Britain as a baby and teaches at the University of Central Lancashire. In 2017 she became the first Black woman to win the Turner Prize.

intro.title: Part of the British Black Arts Movement
intro.text: In the 1980s she was one of its first artists, organising shows of Black women artists at a time when galleries ignored them. In 2026 she represented Britain in Venice.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Flat, bright colour and bold pattern, Black figures as the heroes, and paint on cut-out wood, drawers and found objects. Boats, the sea and women together recur.

questions.q: Where was Lubaina Himid born?
questions.explain: Zanzibar is now part of Tanzania. She moved to Britain with her mother, a textile designer.

questions.q: In 2017 Himid became the first Black woman to win…
questions.explain: She was also the oldest nominee since an age limit was dropped.

questions.q: Which country's pavilion did Himid fill at the 2026 Venice Biennale?
questions.explain: Her show there was called Predicting History: Testing Translation.

questions.q: What did Himid study at Wimbledon College of Arts?
questions.explain: That stage training still shapes her shows, which unfold like scenes in a play.

questions.q: In Between the Two my Heart is Balanced, what do the women discard?
questions.explain: Himid imagined Black women undoing the colonial charts that carved up the world.

lubaina-himid.look: bold painted figures, patterns and cut-outs that retell Black history

el-anatsui.name: El Anatsui

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Anyako, Ghana, in 1944, he taught sculpture for decades at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, and kept his studio there. Huge metal 'cloths' shown in Venice in 2007 made his name.

intro.title: Part of installation art
intro.text: His hangings take a new shape each time they are hung. In 2023 he filled Tate Modern's Turbine Hall with Behind the Red Moon, a sail-like work about the Atlantic slave trade.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Thousands of flattened liquor bottle tops joined with copper wire, rippling like gold kente cloth. His earlier works are carved and painted wood.

questions.q: What does El Anatsui stitch together to make his shimmering hangings?
questions.explain: Discarded aluminium caps and seals, mostly from Nigerian distilleries.

questions.q: In which country was El Anatsui born?
questions.explain: He was born in Anyako in 1944, then worked for decades in Nigeria.

questions.q: Which West African textile do his metal hangings echo?
questions.explain: Kente is a strip-woven Ghanaian cloth with royal roots; his gold, red and black metal recalls it.

questions.q: What joins the thousands of metal pieces together?
questions.explain: The pliable wire lets each work be folded and hung in a new way every time.

questions.q: What did the Venice Biennale award him in 2015?
options: The Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement
questions.explain: Venice had first made him famous worldwide when his works were shown there in 2007.

el-anatsui.look: vast shimmering hangings of flattened bottle tops and copper wire

yayoi-kusama.name: Yayoi Kusama

intro.title: Who was she?
intro.text: Born in Matsumoto, Japan, in 1929, she made her name in New York's avant-garde in the 1960s, then worked in Tokyo until her death in August 2026, aged 97.

intro.title: Part of installation art
intro.text: From 1965 she built Infinity Mirror Rooms: mirrored spaces you step into, where lights or dots repeat forever. Tate Modern's show of them drew almost a million visitors.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Polka dots, nets of tiny repeated loops, pumpkins, and mirrors that multiply lights and your own reflection into infinity.

questions.q: Which pattern is Yayoi Kusama most famous for?
questions.explain: Her dots appear on paintings, pumpkins and as points of light in her mirror rooms.

questions.q: In which Japanese town was Kusama born in 1929?
questions.explain: Her family there grew plant seeds; she later studied painting in Kyoto.

questions.q: To which city did Kusama move in the late 1950s?
questions.explain: She soon stood out in its avant-garde with net paintings, soft sculptures and happenings.

questions.q: Which of her works drew almost a million visitors to Tate Modern?
questions.explain: The show ran from 2021 to 2024, making it Tate's most visited ever.

questions.q: Where did Kusama choose to live from 1977 onwards?
questions.explain: She was driven each day to her studio nearby and kept working into her nineties.

yayoi-kusama.look: polka dots, pumpkins and endless mirrored rooms

ai-weiwei.name: Ai Weiwei

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Beijing in 1957, son of the poet Ai Qing, he grew up in exile and later spent years in New York. Bold art and outspoken activism made his name.

intro.title: Part of installation art
intro.text: In 2010 he covered the floor of Tate Modern's Turbine Hall with about 100 million porcelain sunflower seeds, each sculpted and painted by hand in Jingdezhen.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Old Chinese things remade: Qing dynasty furniture and temple beams, dead trees bolted together, ancient urns. Tradition, mass labour and power are his themes.

questions.q: In which city was Ai Weiwei born?
questions.explain: He was born there in 1957; his family was sent into exile soon after.

questions.q: What were the 100 million 'Sunflower Seeds' made of?
questions.explain: Hundreds of skilled workers in Jingdezhen, China, sculpted and painted each one by hand.

questions.q: Which Beijing Olympic building did he help design?
questions.explain: He advised the architects Herzog & de Meuron, then refused to attend the 2008 Games.

questions.q: In 1995 he photographed himself dropping what?
questions.explain: The ancient urn smashed: a challenge to ideas of value and authenticity.

questions.q: In 2011, for how long was Ai Weiwei secretly detained?
questions.explain: He was held without charge, then released on bail, with officials accusing him of tax evasion.

ai-weiwei.look: antiques and everyday objects remade to question power

doris-salcedo.name: Doris Salcedo

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in Bogotá, Colombia, in 1958, she studied there and in New York and still works in Bogotá. Sculptures that mourn victims of Colombia's violence made her name.

intro.title: Part of installation art
intro.text: In 2007 she split the floor of Tate Modern's Turbine Hall with Shibboleth, a 167-metre crack about racism, exclusion and the experience of migrants.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Everyday things made silent: furniture filled with cement, shoes sealed behind cow bladder, shirts stiffened with plaster. The missing person is felt, never shown.

questions.q: Which country's violence does Salcedo's work mourn?
questions.explain: She was born in Bogotá and still lives and works there.

questions.q: What did Shibboleth (2007) put into Tate Modern's floor?
questions.explain: It ran the length of the Turbine Hall; filled in later, it left a visible line.

questions.q: What fills the old furniture in many of her sculptures?
questions.explain: Made useless, the furniture becomes a quiet monument to lost owners.

questions.q: In Atrabiliarios, whose shoes sit behind stitched cow bladder?
questions.explain: The worn shoes stand for the missing and their families' unresolved grief.

questions.q: In 2016 she became the first winner of which sculpture prize?
questions.explain: She had also won the Hiroshima Art Prize in 2014.

doris-salcedo.look: furniture, shoes and spaces scarred by violence and loss

olafur-eliasson.name: Olafur Eliasson

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Copenhagen in 1967 to Icelandic parents, he set up his studio in Berlin in 1995. The Weather Project at Tate Modern in 2003 made his name.

intro.title: Part of installation art
intro.text: For The Weather Project he hung a glowing half-sun under a mirrored ceiling, in fine mist. About two million people came, many lying on the floor to wave at their reflections.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Light, colour, water, mist and ice used as materials. Mirrors and coloured glass make you notice your own seeing. Climate is a recurring theme.

questions.q: What did The Weather Project seem to bring indoors?
questions.explain: A half-circle of lamps, doubled by a mirrored ceiling, looked like a full sun in the mist.

questions.q: In which city is Eliasson's studio?
questions.explain: He founded Studio Olafur Eliasson there in 1995.

questions.q: What did his Ice Watch put in city streets?
questions.explain: Shown in Copenhagen, Paris and London, the melting blocks drew attention to climate change.

questions.q: What is his Little Sun (2012)?
questions.explain: He launched the solar LED lamp with engineer Frederik Ottesen.

questions.q: In which city was Eliasson born to Icelandic parents?
questions.explain: His parents had moved there from Iceland in 1966, the year before.

olafur-eliasson.look: light, water and weather brought into the gallery

kara-walker.name: Kara Walker

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in Stockton, California, in 1969, she grew up in Georgia and works in New York. Huge cut-paper silhouette scenes, starting with Gone in 1994, made her name.

intro.title: Part of installation art
intro.text: Her silhouettes wrap around whole rooms like old panoramas. In 2019 she built Fons Americanus, a 13-metre fountain in Tate Modern's Turbine Hall about the Atlantic slave trade.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Black silhouettes on white: a polite 19th-century craft for portraits, turned to tell brutal stories of slavery, race and power.

questions.q: Which old craft is Kara Walker best known for using?
questions.explain: Once a genteel form for family portraits, she uses it to show the violence of slavery.

questions.q: Which history does Walker's work most often confront?
questions.explain: Her scenes revisit the American South before the Civil War.

questions.q: Which London monument inspired her fountain Fons Americanus?
questions.explain: She borrowed its form, outside Buckingham Palace, to question how empires remember.

questions.q: Which award did Walker win in 1997, aged 28?
questions.explain: She was one of the youngest people ever to receive it.

questions.q: Her 2014 giant sphinx, A Subtlety, was coated in what?
questions.explain: It stood in Brooklyn's old Domino Sugar Refinery before both were demolished.

kara-walker.look: black cut-paper silhouettes of America's history of slavery

wangechi-mutu.name: Wangechi Mutu

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in Nairobi, Kenya, in 1972, she studied in New York and at Yale, and works between studios in Brooklyn and Nairobi. Big collages of hybrid women made her name.

intro.title: Part of Afrofuturism
intro.text: Her mythic, part-human beings mix African tradition with science fiction to imagine new futures. Critics call her work Afrofuturist.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Female figures pieced together from magazine cut-outs, medical illustrations, paint, glitter and pearls. Later sculptures use bronze, soil and found materials.

questions.q: In which city was Wangechi Mutu born?
questions.explain: In 1972. She now works between Nairobi and Brooklyn.

questions.q: Which technique made Mutu's name?
questions.explain: She builds figures from magazine pictures, medical illustrations and paint.

questions.q: Where did Mutu's four bronze sculptures appear in 2019?
options: On the Met's Fifth Avenue facade
questions.explain: They filled niches that had stood empty since 1902.

questions.q: Which ancient figure did The Seated sculptures reimagine?
questions.explain: Caryatids are female figures that hold up buildings. Mutu freed hers from that load.

questions.q: Which New York museum gave Mutu the 2023 survey 'Intertwined'?
questions.explain: It showed more than 100 works from about 25 years.

wangechi-mutu.look: collaged part-human women made from magazines, paint and myth

cindy-sherman.name: Cindy Sherman

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in 1954 in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, she studied in Buffalo and lives in New York. Her black and white Untitled Film Stills (1977–80) made her name.

intro.title: Part of the Pictures Generation
intro.text: Like other young New York artists raised on movies and TV, she borrowed the look of mass media to question how images shape identity.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Sherman herself in every role, transformed by wigs, make-up and costume. She is model, photographer and director. Colour arrives in the early 1980s.

questions.q: Who is the model in almost all of Sherman's photos?
questions.explain: She is model, photographer and director, changing her look with make-up and costumes.

questions.q: What does each Untitled Film Still look like?
options: A scene from an old movie
questions.explain: They evoke mid-century Hollywood and film noir, but the films never existed.

questions.q: Which magazine commissioned her Centerfolds, then never ran them?
questions.explain: Commissioned in 1981, the editor feared they would be misunderstood.

questions.q: Which star does Sherman play in this 1982 photograph?
questions.explain: The Met says she appears as Marilyn, or Norma Jean, out of her famous role.

questions.q: Which fellowship did Sherman receive in 1995?
questions.explain: She also won the Hasselblad Award in 1999.

cindy-sherman.look: photographs of herself in staged roles and costumes

marina-abramovic.name: Marina Abramović

intro.title: Who is she?
intro.text: Born in Belgrade in 1946, she helped make performance a serious art form in the early 1970s. The Artist Is Present (MoMA, 2010) made her world famous.

intro.title: Part of performance art
intro.text: She uses her body as subject and material, testing physical and mental limits. From 1976 to 1988 she worked with her partner Ulay.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Endurance, danger and stillness. Her live works survive as photos, videos and objects, and are sometimes re-performed by younger artists she trains.

questions.q: In which city was Marina Abramović born?
questions.explain: In 1946, in the former Yugoslavia.

questions.q: What did visitors do in The Artist Is Present (2010)?
questions.explain: For about three months at MoMA, she sat across from strangers, one at a time.

questions.q: In Rhythm 0, how many objects could visitors use on her?
questions.explain: For six hours in Naples in 1974, including a loaded gun.

questions.q: What is she scrubbing in Cleaning the Mirror?
questions.explain: She made it in 1995 for a show in Oxford with the Pitt Rivers Museum.

questions.q: Which London institution gave her a major show in 2023?
questions.explain: The RA says she was the first woman to have a major solo show in its Main Galleries.

marina-abramovic.look: live performances that test the limits of her own body

william-kentridge.name: William Kentridge

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Johannesburg in 1955 to anti-apartheid lawyers, he still lives and works there. Short animated films made from charcoal drawings made his name.

intro.title: Part of video art
intro.text: Since 1989 his films have been shown as projections in galleries, later across many screens. They deal with apartheid, colonialism and their lasting effects.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Grey charcoal smudges and ghostly traces of rubbed-out lines. He draws, films, erases and redraws a single sheet, which he calls 'stone-age filmmaking'.

questions.q: In which city does William Kentridge live and work?
questions.explain: He was born there in 1955 and still works there.

questions.q: Which drawing material does he use for his animations?
questions.explain: He draws in charcoal, films, erases and redraws, frame by frame.

questions.q: Who is Soho Eckstein in Kentridge's films?
questions.explain: Soho and the dreamy Felix Teitlebaum, often seen as Kentridge's alter ego, recur through the series.

questions.q: What were the Casspirs in this print's title?
questions.explain: They patrolled Black townships under apartheid.

questions.q: Where at Tate Modern were eight of his films shown in 2012?
questions.explain: 'I am not me, the horse is not mine' was its first UK showing.

william-kentridge.look: charcoal drawings animated by redrawing and rubbing out

steve-mcqueen.name: Steve McQueen

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in London in 1969 and raised in Ealing, he studied at Chelsea and Goldsmiths. Gallery films won him the 1999 Turner Prize, long before his Oscar.

intro.title: Part of video art
intro.text: He makes films for gallery walls rather than cinemas, alongside photos and sculpture. His feature 12 Years a Slave later won the Oscar for best picture.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Big projections in dark rooms, often silent, close-up and slow. London, history and Black experience return again and again.

questions.q: Which prize did Steve McQueen win in 1999?
questions.explain: He was shortlisted for films including Deadpan and Drumroll.

questions.q: Which McQueen film won the Oscar for best picture?
questions.explain: Released in 2013, it won best picture at the 2014 Oscars.

questions.q: What did McQueen's Year 3 show at Tate Britain in 2019?
options: Class photos of London's Year 3 pupils
questions.explain: Tens of thousands of seven-year-olds, also shown on over 600 London billboards.

questions.q: Who is honoured in Queen and Country's stamp sheets?
options: UK service personnel killed in Iraq
questions.explain: Families chose each portrait. He hoped the stamps would go into real circulation.

questions.q: Which London tragedy is the subject of his film first shown in 2023?
questions.explain: A single aerial shot circles the tower. Copies went to Tate and London Museum.

steve-mcqueen.look: films shown in the gallery as projections, and later feature films

takashi-murakami.name: Takashi Murakami

intro.title: Who is he?
intro.text: Born in Tokyo in 1962, he earned a PhD in traditional Japanese painting in 1993. Cute, colourful characters and the Superflat idea made his name.

intro.title: Part of Superflat
intro.text: He named the movement in 2000, linking old Japanese art to anime and otaku culture. Often compared to Warhol, he blurs art and commerce.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Smiling flowers, wide-eyed characters, mushrooms and skulls in flat, bright colour with crisp outlines. Gold leaf nods to old Japanese screens.

questions.q: In which city was Takashi Murakami born?
questions.explain: In 1962. He later studied traditional Japanese painting there.

questions.q: Which fashion house did Murakami work with from the early 2000s?
questions.explain: He collaborated with designer Marc Jacobs on accessories.

questions.q: Who is Mr DOB?
questions.explain: The bow-tied character looks a little like Mickey Mouse, and like Murakami.

questions.q: Which rapper's 2007 album cover did Murakami design?
questions.explain: He created the cover illustration for the album.

questions.q: What do the mushrooms in Murakami's work often refer to?
questions.explain: His mother saw the blast from afar, and its imagery shaped his childhood.

takashi-murakami.look: smiling flowers, cartoon characters and flat, bright colour

hilma-af-klint.name: Hilma af Klint

intro.title: Who was she?
intro.text: A Swedish painter (1862–1944), trained at the Royal Academy in Stockholm, who earned her living with landscapes and portraits. In private, guided by séances, she began painting huge, colourful abstract pictures in 1906. They are now seen as some of the first major abstract works in Western art.

intro.title: In the news
intro.text: On 19 November 2026 her 1920 painting Ser III No. 5 sold at Bukowskis in Stockholm for about $12.7m. Bukowskis says no artwork has fetched more at auction in the Nordic countries.

intro.title: Look for
intro.text: Circles, spirals, petals and letters in soft pinks, blues and yellows, often in pairs of opposites: light and dark, male and female.

questions.q: Which country was Hilma af Klint from?
questions.explain: Born just outside Stockholm in 1862, she died near the city in 1944.

questions.q: What kind of painting is she now famous for?
questions.explain: Shapes and colours standing for spiritual ideas, started years before most abstract pioneers.

questions.q: What did she ask for her abstract paintings after her death?
questions.explain: She felt the world was not ready for them. She left them to her nephew.

questions.q: In 2026 one of her paintings sold for about $12.7m. In which city?
questions.explain: At the auction house Bukowskis, which says it is a Nordic record.

questions.q: Her circle of women artists who held séances was called…
questions.explain: They believed spirits they called the High Masters guided their work.

questions.q: Before her abstract work, she earned her living painting…
questions.explain: She trained at the Royal Academy in Stockholm from 1882 to 1887.

questions.q: In which year did she paint her first abstract series?
questions.explain: Primordial Chaos, begun in 1906, when she was 44.

questions.q: Her huge series The Ten Largest (1907) shows…
questions.explain: From early childhood to old age, each canvas about 3.2 metres on its long side.

questions.q: In 1908 she met which spiritual teacher, then visiting Stockholm?
questions.explain: The founder of Anthroposophy. She later spent long stays at his centre in Dornach, Switzerland.

questions.q: Which museum's 2018–19 Hilma af Klint show became its most visited ever?
options: Museum of Modern Art, New York
questions.explain: Over 600,000 people came to 'Paintings for the Future'.

questions.q: Which four of these are series from her Paintings for the Temple?
questions.explain: All four belong to the Temple paintings (1906–15). Water Lilies are Monet's, Sunflowers Van Gogh's.

questions.q: In the Temple paintings, what did blue stand for?
questions.explain: Yellow stood for the male spirit, and pink and red for love.

questions.q: Tate Modern in London showed her in 2023 alongside which Dutch painter?
questions.explain: 'Forms of Life' set her beside another painter whose work moved from nature to abstraction.

questions.q: In 1928 she took some of her abstract paintings abroad to a spiritual conference. Where?
questions.explain: She sailed there with some of her large paintings, probably from the Temple series, according to art historian Julia Voss.

questions.q: Which group of her Temple paintings did Rudolf Steiner single out for praise?
questions.explain: Among the paintings she showed him, he picked these as the best in their symbolism.

hilma-af-klint.look: glowing circles, spirals and petal shapes in soft pinks, blues and yellows
